data.title: Living-off-the-Land Binaries Unrestricted
data.summary:
Signed operating system utilities capable of downloading, decoding and executing arbitrary
code were available to standard users and were used throughout the engagement without
detection.
data.description:
The operating system ships with everything an operator needs. Utilities intended for
legitimate administration will fetch a remote file, decode it, and execute it — all
signed by the vendor, all expected on disk, and all permitted by allow-lists built on
publisher trust.

This defeats the common mental model in which attacker tooling is foreign. Nothing foreign
is introduced, so file-based controls have nothing to inspect, and publisher-based
application control explicitly permits the binary.

The discriminator is argument and parent-process context: the utility is not unusual, but
being invoked by a document handler with a URL argument is. That context is only available
if command lines are logged, which is the gap this finding usually comes down to.
data.recommendation:
* Enable command-line process auditing and forward it centrally; without arguments these
  executions are indistinguishable from legitimate ones.
* Block the utilities with no business use on workstations through application control.
* Alert on known abuse patterns — a document handler spawning a script host, a signed
  utility invoked with a remote URL.
* Apply allow-listing with rules that account for interpreter abuse rather than trusting
  the publisher alone.
data.short_recommendation: Log command lines and alert on signed utilities invoked with remote arguments.

attack_techniques.technique: T1127 — Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
